title: Installation Overview
lede: Aegis is delivered as pre-tested modules and assembled on a prepared foundation, sequencing the machine, its shielding, and balance of plant.
body: Aegis is the Kronos burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) in a fixed-installation housing: a D-³He tandem-mirror generator. Installation is the ordered process of turning a prepared site into a commissioned machine. Because Aegis is at the design and simulation stage, the sequence described here is the engineering plan the design is optimized against, not a record of a built unit.

The installation strategy is module-first. The high-field plug assemblies, the central-cell solenoid, the direct-energy-conversion (DEC) end, the cryoplant, and the power skids are factory-built, factory-tested, and shipped as transportable units. Site work is dominated by civil foundations, shielding placement, and inter-module connection rather than in-place fabrication.

A tandem mirror is a linear machine: high-field plugs at each end, a long central cell between them, and an expander tank feeding the direct converter. That linear geometry is friendly to modular assembly — each section has clean mechanical and cryogenic interfaces. Testing coils, vacuum integrity, and instrumentation before shipment removes the highest-risk work from the critical path on site.
Foundation cure and survey tolerance before any coil is set
Radiation-shielding placement, which is heavy and sequence-locked
Cryogenic line routing and leak verification
Alignment of the plug–cell–plug axis to specification
Staged energization: vacuum, then cold, then first plasma

The neutron fraction of D-³He operation is low (5.44%), which reduces — but does not remove — shielding and activation constraints compared with a D-T machine. Installation planning treats the reactor hall as a controlled radiological area from first fuel.

title: Site Selection
lede: Site selection balances structural, thermal, electrical, and access requirements for a fixed low-signature generator.
body: A fixed installation is chosen, not moved. Site selection therefore front-loads the constraints that are expensive to change: bearing capacity for a heavy shielded hall, room for heat rejection, a firm electrical tie or islanded distribution, and controlled access for oversized module delivery.

Aegis is intended to deliver resilient, low-signature, sovereign power for fixed installations. Siting favors compact footprints, restrained thermal and acoustic plumes, and hardened services. The linear machine plus DEC end is arranged so the reactor hall, control building, and utilities form a defensible, screened compound.

Selection fixes the grid or islanded interconnection point, the heat-rejection method, and the fuel-handling location for D-³He. These choices propagate into the balance-of-plant design, so they are locked before civil design proceeds. Because the machine is at design stage, siting studies are performed as engineering scenarios against the frozen tandem-mirror configuration (26.49 T plug, 17 T throat, DEC end).

title: Civil Works & Foundations
lede: The reactor hall foundation carries heavy shielding and precision coil loads, with alignment tolerance driving the civil specification.
body: Civil works create the stable, aligned, shielded volume the machine sits in. The dominant loads are static: the mass of the high-field plug and central-cell coil structure, the radiation shielding, and the cryogenic and vacuum vessels. The foundation is designed for low differential settlement because coil alignment tolerance is tight along the tandem-mirror axis.

A tandem mirror is only as good as the straightness of its magnetic axis. The plug–central-cell–plug line must be held to survey tolerance through machine assembly and thermal cycling. The bedplate and its anchoring are designed so that cool-down of the superconducting coils does not walk the axis out of specification.

Radiation shielding is heavy and its placement is order-dependent — you cannot easily add a shield block after adjacent components are set. Civil design pre-plans shield support, penetrations, and the labyrinths that let cooling, vacuum, and diagnostics pass without creating radiation streaming paths.
Trenches and chases for cryogenic transfer lines
Cable galleries for power and instrumentation
Containment curbs and drainage for tritium-bearing systems
All civil interfaces are frozen against the design geometry before steel is set, because rework in a shielded hall is disproportionately costly in schedule and dose.

title: Modular Delivery & Rigging
lede: Factory-tested modules are transported, received, and rigged into place in a sequence that keeps high-risk work off the critical path.
body: Aegis modules — plug assemblies, central-cell sections, the DEC end, cryoplant skids, and power skids — are built and tested in a controlled factory environment, then shipped to site. Rigging is the choreography of receiving, staging, lifting, and setting these units against survey marks.

The heaviest and largest modules — the high-field plug coil assemblies — define the transport envelope. Route surveys confirm road or rail clearances, bridge ratings, and turning radii before manufacture is released, so a module cannot be built to a size the corridor cannot carry.
Central-cell bedplate set and surveyed first
Plug assemblies set to each end against the axis reference
DEC / expander end aligned to the plug throat
Balance-of-plant skids connected after machine core is set

Vacuum-facing surfaces and cryogenic joints are protected during handling. Modules arrive sealed; internal exposure is minimized and performed under cleanliness control to protect ultimate vacuum quality. Factory acceptance data travels with each module so field teams verify condition on receipt rather than re-testing from scratch.

Because installation is planned from the frozen design, rigging studies use the actual coil masses and geometries of the tandem-mirror configuration; nothing here is built yet, so these are the load cases the design is verified against.

title: Magnet Installation & Alignment
lede: The high-field plug and central-cell coils are set, aligned to the magnetic axis, and prepared for cryogenic cool-down.
body: The magnet system defines Aegis. Two high-field plug coils (26.49 T class) confine the ends, the central-cell coils shape the long burn region, and the throat/expander coils (17 T at the throat) transition to the direct converter. Installation sets these coils to a common magnetic axis and prepares them for superconducting operation.

Alignment is the governing activity. Each coil assembly is positioned so its field center lies on the design axis within tolerance. Optical and laser survey references, established during civil works, are carried through coil setting. Because superconducting coils shrink on cool-down, the warm-set position is offset to land on-target cold.
Coil terminations and current leads connected to the cryoplant
Structural restraints checked for magnetic and thermal loads
Vacuum and thermal-shield closure around each cold mass

After setting, coils are not energized until the cryostat is closed, evacuated, and the cold mass is at operating temperature. The plug coils carry the highest field and the highest stored energy, so their protection systems — quench detection and controlled discharge — are commissioned before any high-current test.

These procedures target the frozen magnet parameters (26.49 T plug, 17 T throat, 8 T on-axis central-cell class). The machine is a design study; installation and alignment are engineered and simulated, not yet performed on hardware.

title: Vacuum Vessel Installation
lede: The vacuum boundary is assembled, sealed, and leak-verified to reach and hold the ultra-high vacuum the tandem mirror requires.
body: A magnetic-confinement machine runs in ultra-high vacuum. The vacuum vessel and its extensions — central cell, plug regions, throat, and expander tank — form a continuous boundary that must be assembled, sealed, and proven leak-tight before any plasma work.

Rough pumping to a mechanical base pressure
Helium mass-spectrometer leak testing of every joint
Documented leak rate against acceptance limits
Bakeout to drive off surface water and adsorbed gas

Ultimate vacuum quality depends on the cleanliness of interior surfaces and the effectiveness of bakeout and conditioning. Handling protocols during rigging protect vacuum-facing surfaces; conditioning later removes the residual gas load. The vessel design and installation target the pressures the D-³He plasma requires for stable central-cell operation.
As with the rest of Aegis, this is the installation plan for a design-stage machine; the vacuum boundary is specified and simulated against the frozen configuration.

title: Cryoplant Installation
lede: The helium refrigeration plant that keeps the superconducting coils cold is installed, connected, and commissioned before magnet energization.
body: The high-field plug and central-cell coils are superconducting, so they need continuous cryogenic cooling. The cryoplant is a helium refrigeration system with compressors, a cold box, distribution lines, and the current-lead cooling that carries away resistive heat at the warm-to-cold transition.

Why it is on the critical path

No coil is energized until it is cold and its protection systems are live. The cryoplant must therefore be installed, leak-checked, and demonstrated capable of reaching and holding operating temperature before magnet commissioning. Its reliability directly bounds machine availability, because a loss of cooling forces a controlled magnet discharge.
Vacuum-jacketed transfer lines to each cold mass

Commissioning proves the full chain: circulate, cool down the cold masses in a controlled ramp, verify temperatures and flow at every coil, and confirm the plant can reject the steady heat load plus transient loads from operations. Cool-down rate is managed so thermal contraction does not disturb coil alignment.
Cryoplant sizing follows the frozen magnet design (26.49 T plug, 17 T throat). The system is engineered and simulated at design stage.

title: Grid & Islanded Interconnection
lede: Aegis can tie to a grid or run islanded, delivering firm power through the direct converter and power-conditioning chain.
body: Direct energy conversion in the tandem mirror produces electrical power from the expanding plasma stream at the DEC end. That output is conditioned and then delivered either to a grid interconnection or to an islanded load. Both modes are designed in from the start because sovereign, resilient supply is the point of a fixed installation.

When tied to a grid, Aegis synchronizes and delivers firm output within the interconnection agreement's protection and power-quality requirements. Switchgear, protection relaying, and metering are standard balance-of-plant scope, sized to the conditioned output rating.

For resilient installation power, Aegis can supply a defined islanded load independent of an external grid. Islanded operation requires the plant to manage its own house load, frequency, and voltage, and to ride through or gracefully shed load during disturbances. This is central to the sovereign-power mission.
Cryoplant, vacuum pumps, and controls draw continuous house load
A blackstart path lets the plant reach operation without external supply
Load-shedding and priority schemes protect critical systems
Interconnection studies and islanding controls are engineered against the frozen machine at design stage; no net-power hardware operation is claimed before the first test burner.

title: Commissioning Plan
lede: Commissioning proceeds in gated stages from cold checkout to first plasma, proving each subsystem before the next depends on it.
body: Commissioning turns an installed machine into an operable one through a sequence of gated milestones. Each stage proves a subsystem in isolation, then in integration, before the next stage relies on it. No stage is skipped, and each has entry and exit criteria.

Between gates, integrated tests exercise the interlock chains, the protection systems, and the control architecture end to end. Fault injection confirms that trips, fast discharges, and safe states behave as designed under realistic conditions rather than only on paper.

Aegis is at the design and simulation stage; the burner is being perfected while the breeder (Hyperion) is built. The first test burner is targeted around 2032. This commissioning plan is the sequence the design is engineered to satisfy, and no hardware net-gain is claimed before it is executed.

body: Site layout organizes the installation into zones that separate hazards, control access, and keep operations efficient. The reactor hall is the innermost controlled zone; power conversion, cryogenics, control, and utilities radiate outward with graded access and protection.

Access is graded: routine operations touch only the outer zones; the reactor hall is entered under radiological controls during outages. Egress routes, muster points, and emergency access for responders are designed into the plan, along with a hardened control building for continuity during upsets.

Consistent with the Aegis mission, the compound is compact and screened, with restrained thermal and acoustic plumes and hardened services. Zoning also supports physical security: the highest-value and highest-hazard areas sit behind the most layers of the compound.
The layout is designed against the frozen linear machine geometry; the installation is a design-stage engineering plan.

title: Balance of Plant Overview
lede: Balance of plant is every system around the reactor core that supplies it, converts its output, and keeps it safe and available.
body: The reactor core — plugs, central cell, throat, and DEC end — does not run alone. Balance of plant (BOP) is the surrounding set of systems that feed it, cool it, convert its output to usable power, and keep it monitored and safe. BOP typically dominates plant part count and much of the operations workload.

Because the burner emphasizes direct energy conversion and a low neutron fraction (5.44%), its BOP differs from a conventional thermal plant: less emphasis on a large steam cycle, more on cryogenics, vacuum, power electronics, and radiological handling of the neutron byproduct. BOP is engineered at design stage against the frozen machine.

title: Direct-Energy-Conversion Balance of Plant
lede: The direct converter turns the expanding plasma stream into electricity, with power electronics conditioning it for delivery.
body: Direct energy conversion (DEC) is the defining efficiency feature of the D-³He tandem mirror. Charged fusion products and plasma leaving the central cell expand along a diverging field into the expander tank, where their kinetic energy is collected directly as electrical current rather than through a heat cycle.

In the expander, the magnetic field weakens toward the DEC end (from the 17 T throat class outward). The plasma stream fans out and its charged particles are decelerated against biased collector stages, delivering current at high potential. This converts particle energy to electricity without an intermediate thermal loop for that fraction.
Collector stages at graded potentials capture the energy spread
Conditioning electronics convert the raw output to grid- or load-compatible power
Protection isolates faults without disturbing the plasma unnecessarily

Because a large share of energy is converted directly, the burner leans on power electronics and high-voltage engineering rather than a large steam plant. Residual heat — including that from the 5.44% neutron fraction deposited in shielding and structure — is still managed by the thermal systems, but the primary conversion path is electrical.
DEC performance figures are design-stage results from the frozen configuration; no net-power hardware operation is claimed before the first test burner.

title: Thermal Management & Heat Rejection
lede: Waste heat from shielding, structure, and auxiliaries is collected and rejected to the environment through the plant's cooling systems.
body: Even with direct energy conversion, Aegis produces waste heat: neutron and gamma energy deposited in shielding and structure, resistive losses in current leads, and auxiliary loads. Thermal management collects this heat and rejects it to the environment while holding components within their temperature limits.

Heat rejection can use dry cooling, wet cooling, or a hybrid, chosen at site selection based on climate and water availability. Dry cooling reduces water use and plume signature — valuable for a low-signature fixed installation — at the cost of larger heat-exchanger area. The method is fixed early because it drives site footprint and layout.

Each cooled subsystem has a control loop that holds it within limits across load and ambient swings. The shield-cooling loop is safety-relevant: it must remove decay and residual heat even during shutdown, so it is backed by emergency power and passive margins where practical.
Thermal loads are computed at design stage from the frozen machine; the plant is not yet built.

title: Cooling Water Systems
lede: Closed and auxiliary cooling loops carry heat from shielding, current leads, and equipment to the heat-rejection system.
body: Cooling-water systems are the intermediate loops between heat sources and final rejection. A closed primary loop serves the components that see radiation — chiefly the shield — and is kept isolated to control activation of the coolant and to contain any contamination. Secondary loops serve conventional equipment.

Loops are separated so that any activated or potentially contaminated coolant stays within a closed, monitored circuit and is not the same water that reaches the environment. Intermediate heat exchangers pass heat between loops without mixing fluids, a standard defense-in-depth practice.
Treatment controls corrosion, scaling, and biological growth
Makeup replaces evaporative and blowdown losses
Monitoring watches for activation, contamination, and leaks
Inventory sized so short supply interruptions do not force a trip

The shield-cooling loop removes heat that must keep flowing even after shutdown, because residual and decay heat persist. It is therefore treated as a supported system with backup power and, where practical, passive circulation margins. Cooling-water design follows the frozen machine's thermal loads and is a design-stage engineering package.

title: Cryogenic Plant Operations
lede: Operating the helium refrigeration plant keeps the superconducting coils cold, stable, and protected across all machine states.
body: Once installed, the cryoplant runs continuously. Its job is to hold the plug (26.49 T class) and central-cell coils at operating temperature, absorb steady and transient heat loads, and support controlled cool-down and warm-up. Cryogenic reliability is a first-order driver of machine availability.

A loss of cooling or a coil quench triggers protection: quench detection initiates a controlled discharge of the coil's stored energy into an external dump, and the cryoplant manages the resulting thermal load. Operations procedures define exactly how the plant responds so that a fault degrades gracefully rather than damaging the magnet.

The plant manages helium inventory — recovering and re-liquefying rather than venting — with storage sized to ride through short upsets. Availability planning treats the cryoplant as a system whose redundancy directly buys machine uptime. All of this is engineered at design stage against the frozen magnet configuration.

title: Electrical Balance of Plant
lede: Electrical BOP manages house load, the conditioned power output, emergency supplies, and protection across the installation.
body: Electrical balance of plant is the distribution, switching, and protection that ties the machine, its auxiliaries, and its output together. It supplies house load to run the plant, routes the conditioned DEC output to delivery, and provides emergency power to safety systems when normal supply is lost.

Metering and power-quality monitoring at the interconnection
Grounding and lightning protection for the compound

Safety-relevant loads — cryogenic protection, shield cooling, controls, and monitoring — are backed by emergency power so that loss of normal supply does not compromise the safe state. Battery-backed uninterruptible supplies bridge the transfer to standby generation. The design follows the frozen machine at design stage and is not yet built.

body: The direct converter produces high-voltage output from the plasma stream. Power conditioning transforms this into the form the grid or the islanded load requires — correct voltage, frequency, and power quality — while providing the protection and control needed for firm delivery.

Aegis is designed for firm, resilient supply. The conditioning chain and controls let the plant hold output steady, respond to load changes, and ride through disturbances. In islanded mode it also sets frequency and voltage for its load rather than following an external grid.

The conditioned output rating follows from the machine's conversion performance, computed at design stage from the frozen configuration. No net-power hardware operation is claimed before the first test burner (~2032). The conditioning and delivery systems are engineered and simulated against that design point.

title: Fuel Handling: D-³He
lede: Deuterium and helium-3 are stored, metered, and injected into the central cell, with unburned fuel recovered and recycled.
body: Aegis burns deuterium and helium-3. Fuel handling is the set of systems that store these gases safely, meter them precisely, inject them into the central cell, and recover and recycle unburned fuel from the vacuum exhaust. Helium-3 is a scarce input, so recovery efficiency matters operationally.

Fuel is stored in a controlled area with inventory tracking. Deuterium is abundant; helium-3 is supplied through the Kronos fuel cycle, including breeder-sourced helium-3, and is treated as a managed, accountable inventory. Metering delivers the fuel mixture to specification for the target plasma composition.
Gas or pellet injection feeds the central-cell plasma
Feedback control trims the mix to hold the operating point
Isolation valves and interlocks govern every fuel path

The vacuum pumping system removes exhaust containing unburned deuterium and helium-3 plus reaction products. Fuel handling separates and recycles the valuable species rather than discarding them, and routes any tritium byproduct to controlled handling. This closes as much of the fuel loop as practical, conserving helium-3.
Fuel-handling design follows the frozen D-³He operating point and is a design-stage engineering package tied to the Kronos fuel supply.

title: Vacuum Pumping Systems
lede: A staged pumping train establishes and holds the ultra-high vacuum, and removes plasma exhaust for fuel recovery.
body: Vacuum pumping does two jobs: it establishes and maintains the ultra-high vacuum the plasma requires, and it removes the exhaust stream during operation so that unburned fuel can be recovered. The train is staged from mechanical roughing pumps to high-vacuum pumps that reach operating pressure.

During operation, the pumps continuously remove particles leaving the plasma — unburned deuterium and helium-3, helium ash, and byproducts. This stream is routed to fuel handling for separation and recycle, and any tritium is directed to controlled handling. Pumping speed and capacity are matched to the fueling rate to hold the central-cell pressure.

Because a loss of vacuum ends operation, the pumping system is designed with redundancy and clear isolation so that a single pump can be serviced without breaking the whole boundary. Vacuum performance is specified at design stage against the frozen machine's operating pressure.

title: Gas Injection & Fueling
lede: Fueling delivers the deuterium and helium-3 mix into the central cell and trims composition to hold the operating point.
body: Fueling is the controlled delivery of fresh fuel into the plasma to sustain the burn and hold the target composition. In a steady-state tandem mirror, fueling replaces particles lost to the ends and to reactions, matching the recovery and pumping systems so density and mix stay on their setpoints.

Fuel can be introduced as gas at the periphery or as pellets that penetrate deeper into the plasma. The method and location affect where fuel deposits and how the density profile builds. The fueling design targets a stable central-cell profile consistent with the plug confinement and the ambipolar potential.
Diagnostics measure density and the D-to-³He ratio
Control adjusts injection to hold the operating point
Interlocks bound the maximum fueling rate for safety
Helium-3 use is minimized through recovery and recycle

Fueling is one lever in the steady-state control loop that also involves heating, pumping, and plug operation. Together they hold the plasma at the design point. Fueling behavior is modeled at design stage against the frozen D-³He configuration; the machine is not yet built.

title: Tritium & Neutron Byproduct Handling
lede: The low but nonzero neutron fraction and any tritium byproduct are contained, monitored, and handled under radiological controls.
body: D-³He burn is chosen partly because its neutron fraction is low — 5.44% for the frozen operating point — far below a D-T machine. Low is not zero: side reactions and the neutron flux produce activation and small amounts of tritium that must be contained, monitored, and handled under radiological controls.

The 5.44% neutron fraction deposits energy and causes activation in the shield and nearby structure. This sets shielding requirements, drives component-lifetime planning, and makes the reactor hall a controlled radiological area. Compared with D-T, activation is greatly reduced, which simplifies maintenance and waste handling — but the systems are still designed for it.
Trace tritium is separated from the exhaust in fuel handling
It is contained in closed, monitored systems
Effluent and area monitoring watch for release

Handling relies on layered containment: closed process systems, a monitored ventilation and detritiation path where needed, and area and effluent monitoring. The design goal is to keep worker dose and any release far below limits. These systems are engineered at design stage against the frozen neutron fraction and are not yet built.

title: Auxiliary Power & House Load
lede: House load runs the cryoplant, vacuum, cooling, and controls; auxiliary power keeps it available across all plant states.
body: House load is the power the plant consumes to run itself — continuously, whether or not it is generating. Cryogenic refrigeration, vacuum pumps, cooling circulation, controls, and instrumentation all draw house load. Auxiliary power systems make sure this load is served in every plant state, including startup and shutdown.

Non-essential loads shed first during supply shortfalls
Transfer to standby supply is automatic for critical systems

Because losing house load can force a magnet discharge and a machine trip, auxiliary power redundancy is an availability investment as much as a safety one. The chart above is illustrative of relative shares, not measured values; house-load engineering follows the frozen design at design stage.

title: Instrumentation & Control Architecture
lede: A layered control architecture separates plant control, machine protection, and safety functions with clear independence.
body: Instrumentation and control (I&C) is the nervous system of the installation. Its architecture is layered so that ordinary plant control, fast machine protection, and safety functions are separated and appropriately independent, following the defense-in-depth principle that a failure in one layer does not defeat the others.

Safety and protection functions do not depend on the normal plant-control system to act. They use independent sensors and logic where required, so that a fault or a cyber compromise of the control layer cannot prevent a trip. This separation is verified during commissioning by fault injection.

Operators work through the plant-control layer with clear indication of machine state, alarms, and the status of protection and safety systems. The architecture is designed at design stage against the frozen machine; it is engineered and simulated, not yet built.

title: Plant Water & Waste Management
lede: Water inventory, effluent, and solid waste are managed with monitoring appropriate to the low-activation D-³He design.
body: Water and waste management covers plant water inventory, liquid effluent, gaseous release paths, and solid waste. The low neutron fraction (5.44%) of the D-³He burn keeps activation and waste volumes modest compared with a D-T machine, but the streams are still monitored and handled under environmental controls.

Solid waste is dominated by activated components retired over the plant's life — chiefly shielding and structure near the plasma. Because activation is low, most components fall into low-activity categories and decay over manageable timescales. Waste is characterized, packaged, and stored under the applicable framework.

Effluent and gaseous release paths are monitored against limits, and any tritium-bearing stream is routed to controlled handling before release. The management plan is engineered at design stage; the environmental performance targets follow from the frozen machine's low-activation design.

title: Startup Sequence
lede: Startup proceeds from a cold, evacuated, safe machine through magnet energization to plasma initiation and the operating point.
body: Startup is the ordered transition from a safe, standby machine to steady operation. Each step confirms readiness before enabling the next, so the plasma is never approached until the vacuum, cryogenics, magnets, and protection systems are verified. The sequence is reversed for shutdown.

The magnets are ramped in a controlled sequence with quench protection live. The plug coils (26.49 T class) and throat coils (17 T) reach their field before plasma work, establishing the mirror field profile that will confine the burn. The ramp is slow enough to respect thermal and mechanical limits.

Plasma is initiated in the central cell, the end plugs are formed to build the confining potential, heating brings the plasma to conditions, and fueling holds composition. The plant then settles at the design operating point. Startup is engineered at design stage; the first test burner (~2032) is where the sequence is first exercised on hardware.

title: Plasma Initiation & Plug Formation
lede: Plasma is initiated in the central cell and the high-field plugs are formed to build the ambipolar potential that confines it.
body: A tandem mirror confines plasma in the central cell using electrostatic potentials built by the high-field end plugs, not just magnetic mirroring. Plasma initiation creates the central-cell plasma; plug formation raises the potential at each end so ions are reflected back into the burn region.

The central-cell plasma is established and heated. Initial fueling and heating build density and temperature toward the range where the ambipolar potential can be sustained. Diagnostics track the plasma from breakdown onward so the sequence can be halted safely if conditions drift.
High-field plugs (26.49 T class) provide the field required at the ends
Heating in the plug region raises the local potential
The resulting ambipolar potential reflects central-cell ions
The throat (17 T) transitions to the expander and direct converter

The end-plug potential is the gate that keeps ions in the central cell long enough to burn. Forming and holding it is the central control challenge of the tandem mirror. Plug formation, the ambipolar potential, and the confinement it produces are modeled at design stage against the frozen configuration; they are demonstrated on hardware beginning with the first test burner.

title: Steady-State Operation
lede: In steady state the plant holds density, temperature, plug potential, and output constant through coordinated feedback control.
body: Steady-state operation is the design intent of Aegis: a continuous burn delivering firm power, not a pulsed machine. Holding steady means balancing fueling, heating, pumping, and plug operation so that plasma density, temperature, and the confining potential stay on their setpoints while the direct converter delivers constant output.

Because the tandem mirror runs continuously, output is firm rather than intermittent. The control system trims the operating point in response to load changes and disturbances, and the power-conditioning chain smooths delivery. This is what makes Aegis suitable as resilient, always-on installation power.

Operation stays inside a defined envelope bounded by machine-protection limits. Approaching a limit triggers control action and, if needed, a trip. The steady-state operating point and its control are established at design stage from the frozen configuration; steady-state burn is a design and simulation result until demonstrated on the first test burner.

title: Normal Shutdown Sequence
lede: A planned shutdown reverses startup in a controlled order, ending in a cold or warm safe state as maintenance requires.
body: A normal shutdown is a planned, controlled transition from operation to a safe state. It reverses the startup sequence: the burn is ended, plasma is safely terminated, magnets are de-energized in a controlled ramp, and the plant is placed in the state required for standby or maintenance.

Stored magnetic energy is managed as it is removed
Cryoplant continues cooling unless a warm-up is planned
Vacuum is held to protect surfaces for a fast restart

The shutdown ends in either a cold standby (ready to restart quickly) or a warm state for maintenance that requires coil warm-up. Residual and decay heat continue to be removed by the cooling systems throughout. The sequence is engineered at design stage against the frozen machine.

title: Rapid Shutdown & Fast Discharge
lede: On a serious fault, protection terminates the plasma and discharges the magnets' stored energy quickly and safely.
body: When a serious fault is detected — a coil quench, loss of cooling, loss of vacuum, or loss of critical power — the machine-protection system acts faster than an operator can. It terminates the plasma and, if required, discharges the magnets' stored energy into an external dump to protect the coils and structure.

The high-field plug coils store large magnetic energy. On a quench, quench-detection logic opens the coil circuit into an external dump resistor, converting the stored energy to heat outside the cold mass. This limits the temperature and voltage the coil experiences, protecting it from damage. The action is automatic and independent of the normal control system.

Following a fast discharge, the plant settles into a safe state: plasma off, coils de-energized, cooling maintained to remove residual heat, and systems monitored. Recovery follows defined procedures after the fault is diagnosed and cleared. These protection functions are designed and verified at design stage and exercised in commissioning.

title: Plug Field Ramp-Up
lede: The high-field plug coils are ramped to the 26.49 T class in a controlled sequence with quench protection continuously live.
body: The plug coils create the highest field in the machine — 26.49 T at the plug, with the throat at 17 T. Ramping them up is a controlled, monitored operation because these coils carry the most current and store the most energy. Quench protection is live throughout, and the ramp respects thermal and mechanical limits.

Field is raised in steps, with time at each level to confirm coil temperature, mechanical response, and protection status before proceeding. The ramp rate is bounded so that mechanical stress and any localized heating stay within limits. The central-cell and throat coils are coordinated so the mirror field profile builds coherently.
Quench detection monitors every coil continuously
The fast-discharge path is armed and tested before ramp
Cryoplant absorbs the ramp's added heat load

At full field the mirror profile is established: strong plugs at each end, a lower on-axis field (8 T class) in the central cell, and the throat transition to the expander. Plasma initiation and plug formation follow. The 26.49 T plug and 17 T throat are frozen design values; the ramp is engineered and simulated at design stage and demonstrated on the first test burner.

title: Conditioning & Bakeout
lede: Bakeout and plasma conditioning drive residual gas from interior surfaces to reach and hold the vacuum quality the plasma needs.
body: Fresh or freshly opened vacuum surfaces hold adsorbed water and gas that would spoil plasma performance. Bakeout heats the vessel to drive off this load, and plasma conditioning further cleans plasma-facing surfaces. Together they bring the machine to the vacuum quality steady operation requires.

Bakeout is planned into installation and into any maintenance that breaks vacuum, because it sets how quickly the machine returns to service.

Conditioning time is a real contributor to how long a vacuum-breaking maintenance activity keeps the machine down, so procedures aim to minimize exposure and streamline the return. Conditioning and bakeout are specified at design stage against the frozen machine's operating pressure requirements.

title: Maintenance Philosophy
lede: Maintenance is designed in: modular components, planned access, and condition monitoring keep outages short and doses low.
body: Maintainability is a design property, not an afterthought. Aegis is built so that components with finite life can be inspected and replaced with planned access, minimizing outage duration and radiation dose. The philosophy blends scheduled maintenance, condition-based intervention, and remote handling where dose requires it.

Scheduled maintenance follows the calendar or run-hours. Condition-based maintenance acts on measured degradation before failure. Corrective maintenance responds to faults. Aegis leans toward the first two, because predicting and planning work protects availability far better than reacting.

Because the reactor hall is a controlled radiological area — even with the low 5.44% neutron fraction — maintenance is planned to keep worker dose as low as reasonably achievable, using remote handling and the hot cell for the most activated components. The maintenance program is engineered at design stage against the frozen machine.

title: Scheduled Maintenance Program
lede: A tiered schedule groups tasks into short online checks and longer outages timed to component life and inspection needs.
body: The scheduled maintenance program groups tasks by frequency and by whether they can be done while running. Frequent, low-impact checks are done online; deeper inspections and replacements are batched into planned outages so the machine comes down as few times as possible for as short a time as possible.

Because breaking vacuum and warming coils are expensive in time, tasks that require those conditions are batched. An outage is planned so that once the machine is opened, all the work that needs that access is completed together, followed by pump-down, bakeout, and conditioning to return to service.

The schedule is built from component life estimates, inspection intervals, and condition-monitoring data. It is engineered at design stage against the frozen machine and refined as operating experience accumulates, beginning with the first test burner.

title: Remote Handling & Hot Cell
lede: Activated components are handled remotely and serviced in a shielded hot cell to keep worker dose low.
body: Components near the plasma become activated by the neutron flux. Even though the D-³He neutron fraction is low (5.44%), the most exposed parts — shielding, first-wall structure, and near-plasma diagnostics — are handled remotely and serviced in a shielded hot cell rather than by direct hands-on work.

Standardized connections — mechanical, cooling, and electrical — let a manipulator disconnect and reconnect a module reliably. The layout and shielding are designed so these operations are feasible and quick.

Remote manipulation for inspection and refurbishment
Characterization before reuse, storage, or waste routing
Connection to remote-handling transfer paths from the reactor hall

The combination of low activation, remote handling, and hot-cell work keeps worker dose far below limits and supports the as-low-as-reasonably-achievable principle. These systems are engineered at design stage against the frozen machine and its activation inventory.

lede: The high-field plug coils are monitored and serviced with attention to superconducting integrity, cooling, and quench protection.
body: The plug coils (26.49 T class) are the highest-stress magnets in Aegis. Their maintenance focuses on the superconducting winding integrity, the current leads and joints, the cooling circuits, and the quench-detection and protection systems that guard them. Most of this work is condition-based, driven by monitoring rather than routine disassembly.

Design therefore aims to make the plug coils long-lived and to keep serviceable elements — leads, instrumentation, cooling connections — accessible without disturbing the winding. Alignment must be preserved through any warm-up and cool-down cycle.

Before any high-current operation after maintenance, quench detection and the fast-discharge path are re-verified. The plug coils' stored energy makes protection integrity non-negotiable. Plug-coil maintenance is engineered at design stage against the frozen 26.49 T configuration; the coils are simulated, not yet built.

title: Throat Coil & Mirror Maintenance
lede: The 17 T throat coils and expander region are maintained to preserve the field profile that feeds the direct converter.
body: The throat coils (17 T) sit at the transition between the central cell and the expander, shaping the diverging field that carries the plasma stream to the direct converter. Their maintenance preserves the field profile and the mechanical integrity of the expander region, which is central to conversion performance.

Downstream of the throat, the expander tank and the diverging field region are inspected for surface condition and alignment, because the geometry sets how cleanly the plasma stream reaches the collector. Any drift in field profile or geometry affects how efficiently energy is captured.

Throat and expander maintenance is coordinated with direct-converter servicing, since they form one continuous path from central cell to collector. Access and remote-handling provisions are designed so the region can be inspected without a full machine disassembly. This maintenance is engineered at design stage against the frozen 17 T throat configuration.

title: Vacuum Vessel Inspection
lede: The vacuum boundary is inspected for leaks, surface condition, and penetration integrity during planned outages.
body: The vacuum vessel is inspected to catch leaks, surface degradation, and penetration wear before they force an unplanned shutdown. Because opening the vessel is costly — it breaks vacuum and requires re-pumping, bakeout, and conditioning — inspections are batched into planned outages and use non-invasive methods where possible.

Helium mass-spectrometer leak testing localizes leaks against acceptance limits. Continuous vacuum monitoring during operation flags a developing leak early, so inspection can target the suspect region rather than the whole boundary. Isolation valves let a region be checked without venting the entire vessel where the design allows.

After any vacuum-breaking work, the region is pumped down, baked, and conditioned before operation resumes. Inspection intervals and methods are set at design stage against the frozen machine and refined with operating experience from the first test burner.

title: Component Lifetime & Replacement
lede: Life-limited components are tracked against neutron fluence and duty, and replaced on planned campaigns before failure.
body: Some components have a finite life set by neutron fluence, thermal cycling, or wear. The low D-³He neutron fraction (5.44%) extends the life of near-plasma parts compared with a D-T machine, but the first wall, near-plasma structure, and some diagnostics are still tracked and replaced before they reach end of life.

Each life-limited component has a tracked budget — accumulated fluence, cycles, or hours. Condition monitoring and inspection confirm the estimate. Replacements are grouped into planned campaigns so that related end-of-life components are exchanged in one outage rather than several.

Life-limited parts are modular and, where activated, handled remotely and refurbished or dispositioned in the hot cell. The chart shows illustrative relative intervals, not measured values; life estimates are computed at design stage from the frozen machine and confirmed with operating experience.

title: First Wall & Plasma-Facing Maintenance
lede: Plasma-facing surfaces are inspected and replaced to manage erosion, deposition, and heat handling in the central cell.
body: The first wall and other plasma-facing surfaces take the direct interaction with the plasma edge and the particle and heat flux it carries. Over time they erode, accumulate deposition, and fatigue. Maintenance inspects these surfaces and replaces components before degradation affects performance or vacuum quality.

New surfaces are conditioned — baked and plasma-scrubbed — before full operation so they do not release gas into the plasma. Inspection and replacement intervals follow the frozen machine's expected fluxes, computed at design stage and refined with operating experience from the first test burner.

title: Condition Monitoring & Diagnostics
lede: Sensors and diagnostics track component and plasma health continuously so degradation is caught before it forces a trip.
body: Condition monitoring is the practice of watching equipment and plasma health continuously so that degradation is detected and acted on before it causes a failure or a trip. It is the backbone of condition-based maintenance and a major contributor to availability, because predicted work is planned work.

Monitoring feeds trend analysis and alarms. A slow drift toward a limit becomes a scheduled task; a fast excursion triggers protection. The historian retains data so operators and engineers can compare against baselines and refine life estimates over the machine's operating history.

Diagnostics are placed during design so condition can be assessed without disassembly, and so safety and protection functions have the independent sensing they require. The monitoring suite is engineered at design stage against the frozen machine.

title: Availability & Capacity Factor
lede: Availability is engineered through redundancy, condition monitoring, and outage batching so Aegis delivers firm, dependable power.
body: Availability is the fraction of time the plant can deliver its rated output; capacity factor also reflects how much energy it actually produces. For a resilient, always-on installation generator, both are first-order design goals. Aegis pursues them through redundancy, condition-based maintenance, and disciplined outage planning.

Availability targets are set from reliability modeling of the frozen machine and its balance of plant. They are engineering objectives at design stage, validated in stages beginning with the first test burner; no operating availability record exists yet because the machine is not built.

title: Reliability & Redundancy
lede: Redundancy in critical support systems lets Aegis ride through a single failure without losing the plasma or the safe state.
body: Reliability is designed in by making systems robust and by providing redundancy where a single failure would otherwise stop the machine or threaten safety. Critical support systems — cryogenics, vacuum, cooling, power, and controls — are arranged so that the loss of one unit does not force a trip.

title: Outage Planning
lede: Outages are pre-planned, scoped, and sequenced so all vacuum-breaking work happens together and the return to service is fast.
body: An outage is a planned shutdown for inspection and maintenance. Good outage planning maximizes the work done per outage and minimizes the days the machine is down. Because breaking vacuum and warming coils are expensive, all tasks needing those conditions are gathered into a single, well-sequenced outage.

During the outage, work proceeds against the plan with change control for anything discovered. After work is complete, the machine is pumped down, baked, and conditioned, and subsystems are re-commissioned in the startup gate sequence before the burn is restored. This recovery time is planned and shortened deliberately.

Each outage is reviewed to shorten the next: what took longest, what could be pre-staged, what could move online. Outage planning is engineered at design stage and matures with operating experience from the first test burner onward.

title: Spare Parts & Logistics
lede: A stocked, cataloged spares inventory and clear logistics keep repairs from waiting on delivery, protecting availability.
body: Spares and logistics turn a repair plan into a fast repair. If a critical part must be ordered and shipped when it fails, availability suffers regardless of how good the maintenance team is. Aegis plans a spares inventory sized to the failure modes that would otherwise extend an outage.

Some components — superconducting coil elements, specialized shielding, custom electronics — have long procurement lead times. These are identified in design and either stocked or ordered against a life-based schedule so a planned replacement is never waiting on manufacture.

Because Aegis is a fixed, low-signature installation, resupply paths and on-site storage are part of the site plan. Spares and logistics are planned at design stage against the frozen machine and refined as reliability data accumulates.

body: Aegis is designed to run with a lean, highly qualified crew. Automation, condition monitoring, and remote handling reduce the routine workload, letting a smaller crew maintain the plant safely — fitting the sovereign, self-sufficient nature of a fixed installation. The staffing model is developed at design stage and validated as the first test burner is operated.

body: The control room is the operational center of Aegis. From it, operators monitor plant and plasma state, execute startup and shutdown sequences, respond to alarms, and coordinate field and maintenance activity. It is hardened for continuity so the plant can be safely managed through disturbances.

body: Operators are trained and qualified before they run the plant, and they requalify on a schedule. The simulator models the tandem-mirror machine and its balance of plant so operators experience realistic dynamics: plug formation, steady-state control, and the behavior of trips and fast discharge. Because faults can be injected safely, crews build the reflexes that keep a real upset from becoming an incident.

Requalification keeps skills current and incorporates lessons from operating experience and design changes. The simulator is also used to validate procedure changes before they reach the control room. Training is developed at design stage; the simulator is built alongside the machine so crews are ready for the first test burner.

title: Shift Operations & Procedures
lede: Written procedures, shift turnover, and clear authority govern every operating state from routine rounds to emergencies.
body: Operations run on procedures and disciplined shift practices. Every routine and off-normal activity has a written procedure; every shift change transfers plant status clearly; and authority for significant actions is unambiguous. This structure is what makes continuous, safe operation repeatable rather than dependent on individuals.

Turnover at shift change transfers a complete, accurate picture of plant status, in-progress work, and any degraded equipment. Logs record events and actions. Two-person verification applies to safety-significant steps so no single error goes unchecked.

Clear lines of authority define who can authorize which actions, and work-control processes ensure equipment is properly isolated before maintenance. This framework is developed at design stage and validated on the simulator and the first test burner.

title: Safety Systems Overview
lede: Aegis safety is layered defense-in-depth: independent protection, passive margins, and monitoring that hold a safe state through faults.
body: Safety at a fixed installation follows defense-in-depth: multiple independent layers so that no single failure leads to harm. Aegis combines independent safety-system logic, machine-protection trips, passive margins, containment, and monitoring. The low D-³He neutron fraction (5.44%) reduces the radiological source term, but the systems are designed for it fully.

A magnetic-confinement burner holds only a small fuel inventory in the plasma at any moment, and stopping fueling or losing confinement ends the burn — there is no runaway chain reaction. The main hazards to manage are stored magnetic energy, cryogenic and vacuum systems, activation, and any tritium byproduct.

Safety systems are engineered and analyzed at design stage against the frozen machine and verified during commissioning by fault injection. The plant is not yet built; these are the safety functions the design is required to satisfy.

title: Machine Protection & Interlocks
lede: Independent interlocks and trips act faster than operators to terminate the plasma and discharge magnets when limits are exceeded.
body: The machine-protection system prevents damage by acting automatically when the plant approaches or exceeds a safe limit. Interlocks block unsafe actions, and trips terminate the plasma and, if needed, discharge the magnets. These functions are independent of the normal control system so a control fault cannot disable them.

Protection uses independent, and where required diverse, sensing and logic so common-mode faults and control-system compromise cannot defeat it. Its correct operation is demonstrated by fault injection during commissioning. The protection system is engineered at design stage against the frozen machine, including the plug (26.49 T) coil energy.

lede: Shielding attenuates the low but nonzero neutron and gamma flux so worker and public dose stay far below limits.
body: Even at a 5.44% neutron fraction, the D-³He burn produces neutrons and secondary gammas that must be attenuated. Biological shielding surrounds the reactor hall so that dose to workers and the public stays far below limits, and activation of nearby structure is controlled.

Reduced waste volume over plant life

During operation the reactor hall is unoccupied and interlocked. Access during outages is controlled by radiological procedures, with the most activated components handled remotely. Shielding is engineered at design stage against the frozen neutron fraction and verified by analysis; the plant is not yet built.

title: Emergency Power & Blackstart
lede: Backup power keeps safety systems alive through a loss of supply, and a blackstart path restores the plant without an external grid.
body: Loss of normal electrical supply must never compromise safety, and a sovereign installation must be able to recover on its own. Emergency power keeps safety-relevant loads running through an outage, and a blackstart capability restores the plant from a dead condition without relying on an external grid.

If a fault also affects the machine, protection drives it to a safe state — plasma off, magnets discharged if required — while cooling continues on backup power to remove residual heat.

Because Aegis targets resilient, sovereign power, it is designed to restart from a de-energized state using its own resources, then supply an islanded load. Emergency-power and blackstart capabilities are engineered at design stage against the frozen machine and demonstrated in commissioning.

title: Fire & Hazard Protection

body: A fusion installation carries conventional and specialized hazards: fire, high-voltage electrical energy, cryogenic systems, oxygen-deficiency from helium, and stored magnetic energy. Fire and hazard protection detects, isolates, and mitigates these so an initiating event does not cascade.

Large helium inventories create an oxygen-deficiency hazard if released into an enclosed space. Oxygen monitoring, ventilation, and access controls protect personnel in the cryogenic zone. Cryogenic surfaces and lines are guarded against cold-contact injury and brittle failure.

High-voltage power-conversion and distribution use isolation, arc-flash control, and grounding. The magnets' stored energy is managed through controlled discharge and access interlocks. Hazard protection is engineered at design stage against the frozen machine and integrated with the overall safety systems.

lede: Area, personnel, and effluent monitoring track dose and any release so exposures stay far below limits at all times.
body: Radiological monitoring confirms that the shielding, containment, and procedures are working — continuously and by measurement, not assumption. It covers area radiation levels, personnel dose, contamination, and effluent, so any deviation is caught and acted on before it approaches a limit.

Monitoring supports the ALARA principle by revealing where dose is accumulating so work can be re-planned to reduce it. During operation the reactor hall is unoccupied; during outages, access is controlled and dose is tracked in real time. The low 5.44% neutron fraction keeps activation and dose modest but does not remove the need for monitoring.

Dose and effluent data are recorded, trended, and reported against limits. The monitoring system is engineered at design stage against the frozen machine's source term and integrated with the safety systems; it is verified during commissioning.

title: Physical Security & Low Signature
lede: Layered physical security and a low thermal, acoustic, and visual signature protect a sovereign fixed installation.
body: Aegis delivers sovereign, resilient, low-signature power for fixed installations, so physical security and a restrained signature are design requirements, not add-ons. Layered security protects the compound, and the plant is engineered to present a small thermal, acoustic, and visual footprint.

A compact linear machine, direct energy conversion, and a dry or hybrid cooling option reduce the thermal plume; the layout and enclosures reduce acoustic and visual signature. Islanded and blackstart capability means the plant does not depend on external infrastructure that would reveal or constrain it.

The combination — self-supplied power, hardened controls, layered security, restrained signature — is what makes Aegis suited to installations that must keep operating independently. Security and signature are engineered at design stage against the frozen machine and site plan.

Monitoring extends to the environment around the compound — confirming that thermal, radiological, and chemical releases have no significant effect. Because the machine emphasizes direct energy conversion and low neutron fraction, its environmental footprint is small compared with conventional thermal generation of similar output.

Effluent and environmental data are recorded, trended, and reported against the applicable limits, closing the loop that the shielding, containment, and treatment systems are performing. Environmental monitoring is engineered at design stage against the frozen machine; the installation is not yet built.
